name: Sarah
bio:
Sarah (originally Sarai) is Abraham's wife and the mother of Isaac, the promised son through whom Israel descended. The New Testament counts her among the women celebrated for faith, one of the few women in the Bible whose own faith is specifically singled out and praised.

## 👤 Identity and Background: From Sarai to Sarah

Sarai was Abram's half-sister as well as his wife (Genesis 11:29; 20:12). She left Ur with him, traveled through Haran to Canaan, and journeyed with him down to Egypt and later to Gerar. God later changed her name from Sarai ("my princess") to Sarah ("mother of nations"), promising that she would bear a son by Abraham and that kings of peoples would come from her (Genesis 17:15-16).

## 📖 Core Story: Years of Waiting, and the Promised Son

1. **Years of Barrenness**: Sarah remained childless for many years, and following the custom of the time, gave her servant Hagar to Abram to bear a child in her place — which instead created lasting jealousy and conflict in the household (Genesis 16).
2. **Laughing at the Promise**: When God promised that the elderly Sarah would bear a son, she laughed to herself in her tent, not believing she could still have a child at her age — to which God replied, "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:10-14)
3. **The Birth of Isaac, the Promised Son**: At ninety years old, Sarah bore Isaac exactly as God had said, declaring, "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me" (Genesis 21:1-7).

## ✨ Key Character and Theological Significance

- **A Model of Faith**: Hebrews says that "through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed... because she judged him faithful who had promised" (Hebrews 11:11).
- **Honest in Her Weakness**: Sarah's laughter and her harsh treatment of Hagar show that her faith was not without flaws — and precisely because of that, her story reflects all the more truly how God's grace upholds even a faltering faith.
- **A Vessel of the Covenant Promise**: Isaac was the promised son of God's covenant with Abraham, making Sarah an essential part of this central thread of redemptive history; Paul in Galatians even uses Sarah as a picture of the "child of promise" (Galatians 4:21-31).

Sarah's story reminds us that God's promises often go beyond what people consider possible — and that God delights to work through a weak, even doubting, faith to accomplish His eternal plan.
